criteria.descriptor: Correctly maps volatile factual knowledge to RAG and stable format/tone to SFT; accurately characterizes fine-tuning as an unreliable, quickly-stale store for changing facts and PEFT/LoRA as the cost-appropriate SFT method for an 8B model; makes no false claims (e.g. that RAG reliably imposes output style, or that fine-tuning dependably stores retrievable facts).

Addresses both requirements, gives a concrete combined recommendation, provides a plan for the weekly-update cadence, covers the risks of the rejected path, and touches evaluation; loses points for omitting the knowledge-freshness plan, the risks, or one of the two requirements.

Justifies each technique by tying it to the nature of the requirement (behavior vs. volatile knowledge) and to trade-offs (cost, forgetting, staleness), rather than asserting choices without reasoning.

Delivers a clear, well-structured recommendation a reviewer could act on: an explicit verdict, a clean split of the two concerns, and a stated integration/eval plan, using the field's vocabulary correctly.

expected_answer_points: Separates the two requirements: format/tone is a stable behavior (SFT-appropriate) whereas the KB is volatile factual knowledge that should not be baked into weights.
Recommends RAG (retrieve at inference, update by re-indexing) for the frequently-changing KB because it stays current without retraining and fine-tuning is an unreliable store for changing facts.
Recommends SFT for the format/tone requirement using a parameter-efficient method (LoRA/QLoRA) on the 8B model rather than full fine-tuning, to cut cost and reduce catastrophic forgetting.
Notes that a few hundred high-quality, correctly-formatted examples (right chat template, loss on completion tokens) can teach style/format but cannot inject an entire knowledge base.

Identifies concrete failure modes of the rejected weekly-retrain-on-KB approach: staleness between retrains, retraining cost/latency, capability regression/catastrophic forgetting, and hallucination when facts change.
Advocates combining SFT + RAG, ideally training on examples that include retrieved context so the model learns to ground answers and to decline when context is absent.
Mentions evaluation on a hold-out set measuring both format adherence and factual grounding/citation accuracy.
common_pitfalls: Endorses fine-tuning weekly on KB dumps to 'teach' the facts, conflating knowledge injection with fine-tuning and ignoring that weights are a poor, quickly-stale store for changing facts.

Treats it as a single problem and picks one technique for both -- 'just fine-tune everything' or 'just use RAG for everything' -- missing that RAG does not reliably enforce output format/tone and SFT does not keep facts current.
Proposes full fine-tuning on the 8B model with no mention of PEFT/LoRA, ignoring the cost and catastrophic-forgetting trade-offs.
Ignores the weekly-update cadence, offering no plan to keep knowledge fresh or assuming retraining latency is negligible.
Recommends RAG but never explains that the SFT data/model must be taught to use retrieved context (and to decline without it), so the two components never actually integrate.
Omits evaluation, or evaluates only format adherence while ignoring factual grounding and citation accuracy.
reference_answer:
The proposal conflates two different needs: teaching a behavior (format + tone) and serving factual knowledge (the KB). These call for different adaptation strategies.

Format and tone are stable, learnable behaviors -- a good fit for supervised fine-tuning. On an 8B model I would use a parameter-efficient method (LoRA/QLoRA) rather than full fine-tuning: it is far cheaper, trains in minutes-to-hours, and largely avoids the catastrophic forgetting that full fine-tuning risks. A few hundred curated transcripts that exemplify the required structure (greeting, resolution steps, compliance disclaimer, escalation) and tone are plausibly enough to teach the pattern; I would format them with the model's chat template and mask the loss to the assistant turns.

The weekly-changing KB is the wrong thing to bake into weights. Fine-tuning is an unreliable mechanism for factual recall, and any facts learned go stale the moment fees/policies change -- forcing a full retrain every week, which is slow, costly, and still lags the data. Instead, serve the KB via RAG: chunk and embed the articles, retrieve at inference, and update by simply re-indexing when content changes. This keeps answers current with no retraining and lets you cite sources.

Crucially, combine the two: build the SFT set so examples include retrieved context in the prompt and answers grounded in that context (and that decline when context is missing). That teaches the model both the house format and how to use RAG context.

I would reject the weekly-retrain-on-KB path for its cost, staleness between runs, catastrophic forgetting, and hallucination risk when facts change, and I would evaluate on a hold-out set scoring both format adherence and factual grounding/citation accuracy.
